intro.title: What is an online teleprompter?
paragraphs: An online teleprompter is a browser-based tool that scrolls your script at a steady, readable pace while you record or speak on camera. It replaces both expensive hardware rigs and heavy desktop software with a page you open in a web browser. That accessibility is why teleprompters have moved beyond TV studios into the hands of YouTubers, podcasters, educators, sales teams and anyone who goes on camera regularly.

Teleprompter Online is built around one idea: the fewer buttons between you and the next take, the better. Paste your script, adjust speed and font, and press play. Mirror mode, fullscreen, landscape lock on mobile, and a short countdown before you begin are all there when you need them — and out of the way when you don't.

Everything runs locally in your browser. Scripts are never uploaded, tracked, or sold. That distinction quietly matters the moment you prepare a confidential briefing, a product announcement, or a client-facing message.

tips.title: Tips for a natural on-camera read
tips.subtitle: A good teleprompter reads with you, not for you. Small habits make the biggest difference in how confident and conversational you sound.

items.title: Rehearse at the real speed
items.body: Do two or three warm-up passes at the scroll speed you'll actually record at. It lets you calibrate both your pace and your breathing before the record light turns on.

items.title: Write for the ear
items.body: Short sentences, one idea per line, contractions where they sound natural. Your script should read the way you talk, not the way you write a formal email.

items.title: Line up with the lens
items.body: Place your phone, tablet or monitor as close to the camera as you can. The smaller the eye travel between your script and the lens, the more you appear to meet your viewer's eyes.

items.title: Use mirror for glass rigs
items.body: If you read through a beam-splitter teleprompter, flip the text horizontally so it reads correctly in the reflection. A single tap turns it on or off.

items.title: Read a line ahead
items.body: Let your eye scan one line before your voice catches up. It sounds more natural than reading the exact word you're on and gives you time to add inflection.

items.title: Aim for one-take reads
items.body: Continuous takes feel less robotic than heavily cut edits. Playback stops automatically at the end of your script so the final beat lands cleanly.

items.q: Will my script still be there if I close the tab?
items.a: Yes. Your current draft and all your prompter settings are saved automatically in your browser, so reopening the page picks up exactly where you left off. Clearing your browser data removes them.

items.q: Can I use this with a physical teleprompter rig?
items.a: Yes. Use the mirror toggle to flip the text horizontally for a beam-splitter teleprompter in front of your camera. You can also flip it vertically for overhead rigs.
It's designed for mobile. You get large touch targets, landscape fullscreen, a tuned default font size, and tap-anywhere pause and resume so you don't have to reach for the controls mid-take.

items.q: Can I control scroll speed while reading?

items.q: Does the teleprompter scroll automatically when I speak?
items.a: Yes — switch on Voice mode and the script follows your speech instead of running on a timer, so pauses and ad-libs don't leave you behind. It needs Chrome, Edge or Safari and microphone permission.

items.q: What file formats can I upload?
items.a: Plain text (.txt), Markdown (.md), Word documents (.docx), rich text (.rtf) and subtitles (.srt, .vtt). Drag a file onto the script box or use the Upload button. Files are read in your browser and never uploaded.

items.q: Can I use it with Zoom, Google Meet or Microsoft Teams?
items.a: Yes. Open the prompter in a browser window and position it just below your webcam, or run it on a second screen or tablet. Share only your meeting app's window, not the prompter, and your notes stay invisible to everyone else.

items.q: How do I use it on an iPad or iPhone?
items.a: Open teleprompteronline.net in Safari or Chrome, paste your script and tap fullscreen. Add it to your home screen to launch it like an app. Mount the device just under your camera lens to keep your eye line natural.

items.q: Can I change the text and background colours?
items.a: Yes. The settings panel has presets for both, plus a custom colour picker. White on black is the classic choice; yellow on black reduces glare, and black on white reads better in a bright room.
Yes, after your first visit. The page is cached in your browser, so you can open the prompter and read your saved scripts without a connection.

items.q: Does the teleprompter stop at the end?
items.a: Yes. Playback gently stops at the end of your script. Press Restart to go back to the top.

howToUse.title: How to use Teleprompter Online
howToUse.subtitle: Get a smoother take in a couple of minutes.

steps.title: Open the prompter
steps.body: Go to teleprompteronline.net. No login, no install. You're already on the prompter page.

steps.title: Paste your script
steps.body: Copy text from any document — Google Docs, Microsoft Word, Notion, plain text — and paste it into the script area.

steps.title: Choose your speed and font
steps.body: Use the speed slider to match your natural pace. Pick a font size that feels comfortable from a reading distance.

steps.title: Turn on mirror mode if needed
steps.body: If you use a glass teleprompter rig, flip the text horizontally so it reads correctly through the reflection.

steps.title: Go fullscreen
steps.body: Tap the fullscreen button for a distraction-free view. On mobile, the prompter will switch to landscape if your device supports it.

steps.title: Press play and record
steps.body: Hit Play (or the Space bar) and start your recording. Use arrow keys or the on-screen slider to nudge speed mid-read.

tips: Do a short rehearsal to find your ideal speed before recording.
Keep a comfortable distance between your eyes and the screen — around an arm's length for phones.
If you're filming with an external camera, place the phone or tablet as close to the lens as possible to preserve eye contact.
Break long paragraphs into shorter lines. Scripts scroll better when each line is readable in one glance.
Save your common intros and outros as named scripts to reuse later.

meta.description: Record sharper YouTube intros, tutorials and vlogs with a free browser teleprompter. Mirror mode, voice-following scroll and keyboard shortcuts included.

youtubers.title: Teleprompter for YouTubers
youtubers.subtitle: Make every take count.

why.title: Why creators love it
items: Cut down on retakes with a steady, predictable scroll.
Look directly at the lens while you read, not down at notes.
Save intros, outros and sponsor reads as reusable scripts.
Works whether you film on a phone or a mirrorless camera.

setup.title: A simple setup
setup.body: Put your phone or tablet directly under your camera lens — the smaller the gap, the less your eyes drift off-centre on playback. Paste your script, set the speed to match your delivery, and press Play. If you use a beam-splitter rig, turn on mirror mode and you're set. For long tutorials, break the script into sections and save each as its own named script so you can reset between takes without scrolling.

intro: A YouTube intro is the twenty seconds that decides whether anyone watches the rest, and it is almost always the part that takes the most takes. A prompter turns that from a memory exercise into a reading one — you keep the energy of take one without losing the wording you spent an hour getting right.

The trick on YouTube specifically is that the read has to stay conversational. Long paragraphs scroll past like a legal notice; short lines with one idea each let you look away, land the beat, and come back. Write your script the way you would say it, then let the scroll do the remembering.

recommended.summary: A talking-head read sits a little quicker than a presentation. Start here and adjust after one rehearsal pass.
recommended.speed: 130–150 wpm. The prompter shows the pace it is actually delivering next to the speed slider — drag until it reads about 140.
recommended.fontSize: 48–64 px if the screen is an arm's length away; go bigger if your camera sits further back.
recommended.display: White on black is the safe default. Turn on mirror only if you read through a beam-splitter rig.

faq.q: Will viewers be able to tell I'm reading?
faq.a: Not if the prompter sits close to your lens and you read a line ahead of your voice. Eye travel is what gives it away, not the reading itself. Keep the device within a few centimetres of the lens and write in short lines so your eyes move less.

faq.q: How long should a YouTube script be?
faq.a: Roughly 150 words per minute of finished video is a good planning figure for a conversational delivery. The prompter shows a live word count and time estimate as you type, so you can trim before you record rather than in the edit.

faq.q: Can I use it while filming on my phone?
faq.a: Yes, but you'll need a second screen — a phone can't run the camera app and the prompter fullscreen at once. Most creators put the script on a tablet or laptop just under the phone.

podcasters.title: Teleprompter for podcasters
podcasters.subtitle: Keep your monologues tight.

why.title: Why podcasters use it
items: Deliver ad reads and intros with consistent pacing every episode.
Stay on-script for structured interviews and solo episodes.
Ideal for video podcasts recorded on a second monitor.
Keep legally exact sponsor wording without memorising it.

setup.title: A comfortable read
setup.body: Set a slightly slower scroll speed and a larger font than you would for short-form video, then place the screen just above or beside your microphone so your head stays square to the camera. Save your intro, outro and each sponsor read as separate named scripts and load them as you reach them — it's faster than scrolling through one long document and it stops you reading last month's advertiser by accident.

intro: Podcasting rewards a loose, conversational voice — right up until the sponsor read, where every word is contractually specific and every stumble costs a retake. A prompter lets you keep the loose register for the conversation and switch to exact wording only where it matters.

It matters more again for video podcasts, where the audience can see you glance down at a script. Putting the words next to the lens keeps your eye line steady across a ninety-minute record without forcing you to memorise anything.

recommended.summary: Podcast delivery is slower and more relaxed than a YouTube intro. Give yourself room to breathe.
recommended.speed: 120–140 wpm. Slower than you'd expect: a relaxed read sounds better than a rushed one.
recommended.fontSize: 56–72 px, so you can read it from a normal seated distance without leaning in.
recommended.display: Warm yellow on black is easier on the eyes across a long record than pure white.

faq.q: How do I keep an ad read from sounding read?
faq.a: Rehearse it once at the exact scroll speed you'll record at, then mark your own breath points with line breaks. Reading a line ahead of your voice is what gives you room to add inflection rather than just pronouncing words.

faq.q: Can I use it with Riverside, Zencastr or SquadCast?
faq.a: Yes. The prompter is just a browser page, so run it in a separate window or on a second screen next to your recording tab. Nothing needs to be installed or connected.

faq.q: Is it useful for a two-host show?
faq.a: For anything scripted, yes — put the prompter on a shared screen both hosts can see, or open it on each host's own device. Each device keeps its own scroll position and settings.

presenters.title: Teleprompter for presenters
presenters.subtitle: Deliver keynotes with confidence.

why.title: Why presenters use it
items: Keep your eyes on the camera during webinars and town halls.
Never lose your place in long keynote scripts.
Run it on a second monitor or tablet while you present.
Hold to approved wording for legal, financial or medical content.

setup.title: Pro delivery in minutes
setup.body: Paste your script, dial in a calm scroll speed, and go fullscreen on a secondary screen positioned as close to the camera or audience eye line as the room allows. Do one rehearsal pass at the real speed before you go live — it calibrates your breathing as much as your pace. If your talk has a Q&A section, stop the prompter at the end of the scripted part rather than leaving it scrolling.

intro: The hard part of a keynote is not knowing the material — it is holding the room while remembering the exact phrasing your team spent two weeks approving. A prompter takes the memory load off so your attention can go to pace, emphasis and the people in front of you.

For webinars and recorded internal comms the value is even plainer: nobody is in the room, the camera is unforgiving about where you are looking, and a second screen with your script solves both problems at once.

recommended.summary: Presentation delivery is the slowest of the common use cases — authority comes from unhurried pacing.
recommended.speed: 110–130 wpm. If you feel rushed, the scroll is too fast, not your delivery too slow.
recommended.fontSize: 64–80 px when the screen sits further away, as it usually does on a lectern or second monitor.
recommended.display: Black on white reads better under bright stage or conference-room lighting than white on black.

faq.q: Can I use it while sharing my screen?
faq.a: Yes. Share only the window or tab holding your slides, never your whole desktop, and keep the prompter in a separate window. Your audience sees the deck; you see the script.

faq.q: What if I go off-script during a keynote?
faq.a: Press Space to pause, say what you need to say, and press it again to pick up where you left off. Voice mode handles this even more gracefully — the script waits and follows you back in when you return to the written wording.

faq.q: Will it work on a lectern screen or confidence monitor?
faq.a: Yes. Open the page on whatever device drives that screen and go fullscreen. If the monitor is mirrored through glass, flip the text with mirror mode.

teachers.title: Teleprompter for teachers
teachers.subtitle: Consistent delivery, every lesson.

why.title: Why educators use it
items: Record course intros and lessons with a steady, even pace.
Reuse standard scripts across multiple classes and terms.
Keep your energy up without stumbling on the next line.
Scripts stay on your own device — useful under school data rules.

setup.title: Classroom-ready
setup.body: Save a standard intro as a script, load it before each lecture, adjust the font for your camera distance and press Play. For a whole module, keep one script per lesson with a clear name — the saved list shows when each was last edited, which makes it easy to see what you've already refreshed this term. Everything stays in your browser on your own machine, so no student-facing material passes through a third-party server.

intro: Recording course material is a different job from teaching a room. There is no class to read, no questions to react to, and every stumble is a cut you will have to make later. A prompter restores the one thing a live room gives you for free: a reason to keep going forward.

It also solves the repetition problem. If you teach the same module every term, a saved script means this year's recording matches last year's in structure and length, and you only re-record the parts that actually changed.

recommended.summary: Teaching delivery wants clarity over speed. Err slower than feels natural on the first pass.
recommended.speed: 115–135 wpm, slower still for technical material students need time to absorb.
recommended.fontSize: 56–72 px so you can stand back from the screen and still gesture naturally.
recommended.display: White on black for a darkened recording room; black on white if you film in a bright classroom.

faq.q: Does my script get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Saved scripts and your current draft stay in your browser's local storage on the device you used. Nothing is sent to a server, which usually makes this straightforward under institutional data policies — though your own institution's rules are the ones that decide.

faq.q: Can I use it for live online classes?
faq.a: Yes. Run it in a window beside your video call and share only the meeting window. It works well for the scripted opening of a class, then you can pause it and teach normally.

faq.q: How do I keep lectures to a consistent length?
faq.a: Watch the word count and time estimate above the script box as you write. They update as you type and reflect your current scroll speed, so you can plan a fifteen-minute lesson before recording rather than discovering the length afterwards.

meta.title: Teleprompter for Streamers – Notes During Live Broadcasts
meta.description: Use Teleprompter Online during live streams to glance at talking points, sponsor reads and CTAs without breaking eye contact.

streamers.title: Teleprompter for streamers
streamers.subtitle: Notes on demand, without breaking eye contact.

why.title: Why streamers use it
items: Open it on a second screen during your live broadcast.
Save sponsor reads and calls to action for quick recall.
Keep pacing natural even during long sessions.
Pause and resume instantly when chat pulls you off-script.

setup.title: Fit it to your stream
setup.body: Dock the prompter on a secondary monitor near your camera, sized so you can read it peripherally without turning your head. Keep it paused by default and press Space when you reach a sponsor read. Use the light theme in a bright room and the dark theme at night — a glowing white window off-camera will show up in your face lighting. Save each recurring segment as its own script so you can load one in a couple of seconds between scenes.

intro: Live streaming is mostly improvised, and that is the point — but the parts that aren't improvised are usually the parts that pay. Sponsor reads, campaign call-outs and the segment structure you promised your audience all benefit from being written down where you can see them.

The challenge is that a stream has no retakes. What you need is not a script to read start to finish but a set of prompts you can drop into at the right moment, which is exactly what saved scripts and a pause-anywhere scroll are for.

recommended.summary: A stream prompter is glanced at, not read continuously — favour large text you can catch in half a second.
recommended.speed: Leave it paused by default and press Space at a scripted beat; 110–130 wpm when it runs.
recommended.fontSize: 64 px and up. You're reading from across a desk, at a glance, while doing something else.
recommended.display: White or yellow on black so a bright prompter window doesn't wash out your face on camera.

faq.q: Will the prompter show up in my stream capture?
faq.a: Only if you capture that display or window. Capture your game or camera source specifically rather than a full monitor, and the prompter stays off-stream.

faq.q: Can I control it without alt-tabbing?
faq.a: Keyboard shortcuts work whenever the prompter window has focus. Many streamers put it on a second monitor and click it once before a scripted segment; a stream deck can also be bound to send the Space key.

faq.q: Does it work alongside OBS or Streamlabs?
faq.a: Yes. It's a browser page with no capture, no hotkey grabbing and no background process, so it sits alongside broadcasting software without interfering.

zoom.title: Teleprompter for Zoom and video calls
zoom.subtitle: Your notes, right next to the lens.
intro: Everyone on a video call can tell when you are reading from somewhere else on the screen. Your eyes track sideways, you go quiet at the wrong moments, and a well-prepared pitch starts to look like a hostage note. The fix is not to prepare less — it is to put the words where your camera already is.

A browser teleprompter positioned just under your webcam keeps your gaze within a few degrees of the lens. For a sales pitch, an interview panel, a board update or a webinar, that small change is the difference between reading at people and talking to them.

why.title: Why it works for video calls
items: Keep your eyes on the lens instead of tracking across the screen.
Works with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex and any browser call.
Nothing to install — useful on locked-down work laptops.
Your notes stay invisible to everyone else on the call.

setup.title: Setting it up in a minute
setup.body: Open the prompter in its own browser window and resize it into a narrow strip directly beneath your webcam — top of the screen, not the bottom, so your eyes stay level with the lens. Start your call as usual. When you share your screen, share the specific application window for your slides rather than the entire desktop, and the prompter stays private. If your laptop camera sits at the top of the display, put the prompter window immediately below it and drag it as narrow as it will comfortably go.

recommended.summary: Call delivery should sound spontaneous, so keep the prompter small, close to the lens, and slower than you think.
recommended.speed: 120–140 wpm. On a call you want to sound like you're thinking, not reciting.
recommended.fontSize: 32–48 px — smaller than usual, because the window sits close to your face and needs to stay narrow.
recommended.display: Match your room: white on black in a dim home office, black on white if you're lit by a window.

faq.q: Can other people on the call see my teleprompter?
faq.a: Not unless you share it. Share a specific window or tab rather than your whole screen, and the prompter window is never transmitted. In Zoom, that's the application window option; Meet and Teams offer the same choice.

faq.q: Does it work on a locked-down work laptop?
faq.a: Usually yes, because there is nothing to install — it runs in the browser you already have. Voice mode additionally needs microphone permission, which some managed devices restrict; every other feature works without it.

faq.q: Where exactly should I put the window?
faq.a: Directly under your webcam, and as narrow as you can read comfortably. Eye travel is what people notice: a tall window makes your eyes visibly scan up and down, while a narrow strip near the lens looks like normal thinking.

mobile.title: Teleprompter for iPhone, iPad and Android
mobile.subtitle: A prompter on the device you already film with.
intro: Phone and tablet screens make excellent teleprompters. They are bright, they are exactly the right size to sit under a camera, and you already own one. What has usually been missing is software that doesn't want an install, an account and a subscription before it will scroll a page of text.

Because Teleprompter Online is a web page, your device already has everything it needs. Open it in Safari or Chrome, add it to your home screen if you want it to launch like an app, and it works offline after the first visit.

why.title: Why mobile works so well
items: No app to install and no account — it runs in Safari or Chrome.
Landscape fullscreen with a tuned default font size for small screens.
Tap anywhere on the text to pause and tap again to resume mid-take.
Add it to your home screen and it opens like a native app, offline.

setup.title: Getting set up on iOS or Android
setup.body: Open teleprompteronline.net in Safari or Chrome, paste your script, and tap fullscreen — the page switches to landscape where the device allows it. To keep it one tap away, use Share then Add to Home Screen on iOS, or Install app in Chrome on Android. Mount the device just below your camera lens; a cheap phone clamp on the same tripod is enough. If you're filming on the same phone you're reading from, you'll need a second device, since no phone can run the camera and a fullscreen prompter at once.

recommended.summary: Small screens fit fewer words per line, so the same scroll number delivers a slower read. Set the pace by the words-per-minute readout, not the slider value.
recommended.speed: 130–150 wpm. Watch the pace readout rather than the raw number: a narrow phone screen fits fewer words per line, so it needs a higher px/s for the same delivery.
recommended.fontSize: 36–48 px on a phone, 56–72 px on a tablet used as a camera-side prompter.
recommended.display: White on black to keep screen glare off your face, which matters more on a device this close.

faq.q: Is there an app to download?
faq.a: No, and that's deliberate. It runs in your mobile browser, so there is no install, no App Store account and no update to chase. Adding it to your home screen gives you an app icon that opens straight into the prompter.

faq.q: Does it work offline on a phone?
faq.a: Yes, after your first visit. The page is cached on your device, so you can open the prompter and read your saved scripts on a shoot with no signal.

faq.q: Can I film and read on the same phone?
faq.a: Not at the same time — the camera app and a fullscreen browser can't both own the screen. Use a second phone or a tablet for the script, or film on a separate camera with your phone as the prompter.

short-form-video.title: Teleprompter for TikTok, Reels and Shorts
short-form-video.subtitle: Nail the hook in one take.
intro: Short-form video is unforgiving in a very specific way: the first three seconds decide everything, and there is no room to warm up. That makes it the format where scripting pays off most and where fumbling the opening line costs you the most takes.

The catch is that short-form also has to look unscripted. A prompter helps here precisely because it lets you stop thinking about what comes next — the mental bandwidth you get back is what makes the delivery feel casual.

why.title: Why short-form creators use it
items: Land the first three seconds exactly as written, take after take.
Keep a 30-second script to 30 seconds using the live time estimate.
Film vertically with the script directly under the lens.
Batch a week of clips without relearning each script.

setup.title: A vertical-video setup
setup.body: Stand your phone in portrait on a small tripod and put the prompter on a second device immediately behind or below it, as close to the lens as you can get. Write in short lines — one thought per line reads far better at speed than full paragraphs. Use the word count and time estimate to trim to length before you shoot, since a script that runs six seconds long is a re-record rather than an edit. For a batch session, save each clip's script by name and load them one after another.

recommended.summary: Short-form delivery is faster and punchier than any other format — and the scripts are short enough to rehearse properly.
recommended.speed: 160–180 wpm. Short-form energy is genuinely quicker than a talking-head video.
recommended.fontSize: 40–56 px, kept narrow so a vertical shot doesn't push the text out of your eye line.
recommended.display: High contrast, white on black. You're often filming handheld in changing light.

faq.q: How many words is a 30-second TikTok?
faq.a: Around 70 to 80 words at a normal speaking pace, less if you want pauses for emphasis. The live time estimate above the script box updates as you type, so you can cut to length before filming instead of after.

faq.q: Can I use it filming vertically?
faq.a: Yes. The prompter fills whatever screen it's on, so a second phone held or clamped in portrait works well. Keep the reading line as close to the filming lens as possible.

faq.q: Will it help with the hook specifically?
faq.a: That's where it earns its keep. Write three variants of your opening line, save each as a script, and shoot all three back to back — comparing real takes beats guessing which hook lands.

meta.title: Teleprompter for Wedding Speeches and Toasts – Free
meta.description: Deliver a best man, maid of honour or father-of-the-bride speech without cue cards. A free teleprompter for your phone, with a timer to keep it to length.

wedding-speeches.title: Teleprompter for wedding speeches
wedding-speeches.subtitle: Say it the way you wrote it at 2am.
intro: A wedding speech is the highest-stakes public speaking most people ever do, delivered to a room of people who love you, usually after a drink, from a folded piece of paper that has been in a jacket pocket all day. The paper is the weak link. It rustles, it's hard to read in dim light, and looking down at it breaks exactly the eye contact that makes a toast land.

A phone held at chest height with large, slowly scrolling text solves all three. You keep the wording you agonised over, you keep your head up for the punchlines, and you can see it in a candlelit room.

why.title: Why it works for speeches
items: Read from your phone instead of shuffling cue cards.
Large, bright text stays readable in dim reception lighting.
Keep your head up for the moments that matter.
The time estimate keeps you honest about length.

setup.title: On the night
setup.body: Load your speech before dinner and check it scrolls at a comfortable pace, because the room will be louder and you will be quicker than in your kitchen. Hold the phone at chest height rather than in front of your face, and pause with a tap whenever the room laughs — a toast that waits for its laughs always lands better than one that talks over them. Aim for three to five minutes: the time estimate above the script box tells you where you are before you stand up, and it beats finding out at the microphone.

recommended.summary: A toast is slower than any other kind of read. Nerves speed everyone up, so set the scroll slower than feels right.
recommended.speed: 100–120 wpm. Slower than you think — you will speak faster on the night than in rehearsal.
recommended.fontSize: 48–64 px so you can hold the phone at chest height rather than up near your face.
recommended.display: White on black, screen brightness up. Reception rooms are darker than you remember.

faq.q: How long should a wedding speech be?
faq.a: Three to five minutes is the sweet spot — roughly 450 to 750 words. The word count and time estimate update as you write, so you can cut before the day rather than mid-toast.

faq.q: Won't reading from a phone look impersonal?
faq.a: Less than you'd expect, and far less than reading from cards. Hold the phone at chest height, look up for every punchline, and let the scroll handle the wording. Guests notice eye contact, not the device.

faq.q: What if I get emotional and lose my place?
faq.a: Tap the screen to pause; tap it again when you're ready. Nothing scrolls away while you take a moment, and the highlighted reading line shows you exactly where you stopped.

meta.title: Teleprompter for Interviews and Self-Tapes – Free
meta.description: Prepare for job interviews, self-tape auditions and recorded intros with a free browser teleprompter. Keep your answers structured and your eyes on the camera.

interviews.title: Teleprompter for interviews and self-tapes
interviews.subtitle: Structured answers, natural delivery.
intro: Remote interviews and self-tapes ask you to be word-perfect and relaxed at the same time, on camera, usually alone in a room. Notes off to the side make your eyes wander; memorising makes you stiff. A prompter under the lens is the compromise that actually works.

The right amount of scripting here is less than you'd think. Full answers word-for-word sound recited; a structured skeleton — the opening line, the three points, the number you must not get wrong — gives you a spine to improvise around.

why.title: Why candidates and actors use it
items: Keep prepared answers structured without sounding recited.
Hold your eye line on the lens for self-tape auditions.
Load a fresh script between takes in a couple of seconds.
Nothing is uploaded, so your notes stay yours.

setup.title: Preparing your script
setup.body: Write prompts, not paragraphs: a bolded question, then three or four short lines under it. Save one script per likely question so you can load the right one between takes rather than scrolling to find it. Position the screen immediately under your webcam or camera lens, and keep the prompter paused by default — press Space only when you want it to move. For self-tapes, do one rehearsal pass at the real speed so your reader's lines and yours stay in rhythm.

recommended.summary: Interview delivery should sound thought-through, not read out. Keep the script sparse and the scroll slow.
recommended.speed: Leave it paused for most answers and start it when you need to; 110–130 wpm when it runs.
recommended.fontSize: 36–52 px, sized so a glance takes in a whole line without a visible eye sweep.
recommended.display: Whatever matches your room lighting — you want the screen not to reflect in your glasses.

faq.q: Is using a teleprompter in an interview dishonest?
faq.a: For notes and structure, no — it's the same as having a page of prepared points, which interviewers expect. Reading full answers verbatim is what gets noticed, and it sounds worse anyway. Keep it to prompts.

faq.q: Does it work for self-tape auditions?
faq.a: Yes, and it's a common use. Put the script just under the lens so your eye line stays right, and pause between takes. Many actors use it for the reader's lines as well as their own.

faq.q: Will an interviewer notice I'm reading?
faq.a: Only if your eyes travel. Keep the prompter directly under the camera, use large text so each line is one glance, and look at the lens between points rather than at the words continuously.

meta.title: Privacy policy – Teleprompter Online
meta.description: How Teleprompter Online handles your data. Spoiler: we don't collect your scripts.

sections.title: The short version
sections.body: Teleprompter Online is a static web app that runs entirely in your browser. We don't create accounts, we don't receive your scripts, and we don't sell data.

sections.title: What stays on your device
sections.body: Your saved scripts, the draft you're currently editing, and every prompter setting (speed, font, colours, mirror, countdown) are stored in your browser's local storage on the device you used. Clearing your browser data will remove them. None of it is ever uploaded to a server.

sections.title: Analytics & cookies
sections.body: We use Google Analytics 4 (measurement ID G-8W0LZYG5VX) and Pageview.app to understand aggregate site usage such as page views and referrers. Google Analytics sets first-party cookies (e.g. _ga, _ga_*) to count unique visitors; Pageview.app is a lightweight, cookieless analytics service. Neither service receives the content of your teleprompter scripts. You can opt out of Google Analytics via the official browser add-on or by enabling "Do Not Track" / Global Privacy Control in your browser.

sections.title: Third parties
sections.body: The site is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Cloudflare may log infrastructure-level request data (such as IP addresses) for security and abuse prevention. Analytics data is processed by Google (Google Analytics) and by the operators of Pageview.app.

sections.title: Voice mode and your microphone
sections.body: Voice mode is off unless you turn it on, and your browser will ask permission before the microphone is used. The script text itself is matched against your speech locally in the page and is never transmitted. The audio is a separate matter: most browsers, including Chrome, send it to their own speech-recognition service to transcribe it, so that audio is handled under your browser vendor's privacy policy. If you would rather no audio leave your device, leave voice mode off — every other feature works without it.

sections.body: Questions about privacy? Email us at hello@teleprompteronline.net or use the contact page.

meta.title: About Teleprompter Online
meta.description: Who builds Teleprompter Online, why it's free, and the principles behind a teleprompter that runs entirely in your browser.

about.title: About Teleprompter Online
about.subtitle: A free teleprompter built on one idea: fewer buttons between you and the next take.

sections.title: Why this exists
sections.body: Teleprompters used to mean a studio, an operator and a rig that cost more than the camera. Then they meant desktop software with a licence key. Neither made sense for someone recording a course intro at a kitchen table on a Tuesday night. Teleprompter Online is the version of that tool we wanted: open a page, paste a script, press play.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Everything runs in your browser. The scrolling engine, the mirror transform, the file import, the saved scripts — all of it is JavaScript executing on your own device. There is no backend that reads your words, because there is no backend at all: the site is a set of static files served from a CDN.

sections.title: What we mean by private
sections.body: Your script, your current draft and your prompter settings are stored in your browser's local storage. They are not uploaded, not backed up to a server, and not readable by us. The trade-off is honest: clear your browser data and they're gone. We think that's the right trade for a tool people use to rehearse product announcements and confidential briefings.

sections.title: Free, and why
sections.body: The site costs very little to run because it does so little on the server side. There's no per-user cost to cover, so there's no paywall, no watermark, no export limit and no trial. If that changes, it will change in the open — not by quietly gating features you already rely on.

sections.title: Built for six languages
sections.body: The interface and every page are available in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German and Italian, with real translations rather than machine output dropped into a template. If something reads wrong in your language, tell us — that's the kind of bug report we most want.

meta.title: Contact – Teleprompter Online
meta.description: Get in touch about bugs, feature requests, translation fixes or press enquiries.

contact.title: Contact
contact.subtitle: Questions, bugs and ideas all reach the same inbox.

sections.title: Email
sections.body: Write to us at the address below and we'll read it. We're a small team, so a reply usually takes a couple of days rather than a couple of hours.

sections.title: Reporting a bug
sections.body: The most useful reports name your browser and device, what you expected, and what happened instead. If the prompter misbehaved mid-read, the scroll speed and font size you were using help a lot — those two settings explain a surprising share of issues.

sections.title: Feature requests
sections.body: Tell us what you were trying to do, not just the feature you have in mind. Knowing the job you're hiring the prompter for is what tells us whether a new button is the right answer.

sections.title: Translations
sections.body: If a phrase reads awkwardly in your language, or a page still shows English text where it shouldn't, send the page address and the wording you'd use instead.

sections.title: Privacy questions
sections.body: For anything about data handling, see the privacy policy first — it covers what's stored, where, and what the analytics do. If it doesn't answer your question, ask.

meta.title: Script Timer – How long will my speech take to read?
meta.description: Paste your script and see exactly how long it takes to say out loud. Free reading time calculator with adjustable speaking pace, then open it straight in the teleprompter.

scriptTimer.title: Script timer
scriptTimer.subtitle: Paste your script and find out how long it really takes to say.
scriptTimer.placeholder: Paste or type your script here to see how long it takes to read aloud…
scriptTimer.scrollHint: Open this in the teleprompter and it sets the scroll speed to match this pace on your screen.

sections.title: Why word count beats page count
sections.body: A page of text can be anything from 250 to 600 words depending on font and spacing, which is why "two pages" tells you almost nothing about how long you'll be talking. Words per minute is the only measure that survives a change of formatting, and it's the one broadcast and conference producers have used for decades.

sections.title: What speaking pace should you use?
sections.body: Most people land between 130 and 150 words per minute in conversation. Formal presentations run slower, around 110 to 130, because pauses do real work in a room. Short-form video and advertising reads push past 160. If you're unsure, record yourself reading for one minute and count — your own number beats any average.

sections.title: Build in time you're not speaking
sections.body: The calculator measures speech, not silence. A wedding toast has to leave room for laughter; a keynote needs beats after each point; a demo has to wait for something to load. As a rule of thumb, add fifteen to twenty percent on top of the spoken figure for anything delivered to a live audience.

sections.title: From estimate to actual take
sections.body: The estimate gets you close, but the only real test is reading it out loud at the pace you'll use. Open the script in the teleprompter, set the suggested scroll speed and do one full pass. If you finish early or run long, adjust and note the speed that worked — it'll be roughly right for everything you write from now on.

faq.q: How many words is a 5-minute speech?
faq.a: Around 650 to 750 words at a normal speaking pace of 130–150 words per minute. Slow down for a formal or emotional delivery and 600 words can fill five minutes comfortably.

faq.q: How long does it take to read 1,000 words?
faq.a: About 7 minutes at 140 words per minute. At a slow, deliberate 110 words per minute it's just over 9 minutes; at a fast 170 it's under 6.

faq.q: How many words is a 30-second video?
faq.a: Roughly 70 to 80 words. Short-form delivery runs faster than conversation, but you still want room for a pause before the payoff.

faq.q: Is speaking time the same as reading time?
faq.a: No. Silent reading runs about 240 words per minute — far faster than anyone speaks. This calculator measures reading aloud, which is what matters for video, speeches and presentations.

faq.q: Does it work for languages other than English?
faq.a: The word count works for any language that separates words with spaces, and Chinese, Japanese and Korean text is counted by character with an adjustment. Speaking rates do differ by language, so trust a one-minute recording of your own voice over the default.
